newsitem.title: TURKEY: Millers, traders worried by U.S.-Turkey wheat row.
newsitem.headline: Millers, traders worried by U.S.-Turkey wheat row.

text.p: Turkish millers and traders expressed concern on Friday that they might lose the United States as a major grain supplier after Ankara's crackdown on U.S. wheat imports and an ensuing U.S. ban on shipments.
"How will we be able to get good wheat with strict regulations like that, which you cannot find anywhere else in the world?" asked an angry miller, who declined to be named.
"The government should be logical and should not seek unrealistic standards for what it imports," he told Reuters.
The United States is a main supplier of grain for Turkey, accounting for about half of all wheat imports. Total imports this year are expected to surpass two million tonnes.

But two weeks ago Turkey held up three cargoes of U.S. milling wheat, saying they were being inspected for ergot fungus, which in large quantities can be toxic to man and animals but occurs naturally in a wide range of cereal products.

Turkey was then enforcing a zero-tolerance limit for ergot fungus in its Food Quarantine Act, but backed down this week by raising the limit to 0.02 percent after criticism from U.S. officials and from domestic traders and millers who depend on imported higher-quality wheat for flour production.

Millers, U.S. farm officials and traders say the new Turkish limit is still too stringent and would make it difficult for Turkey to moderate rises in local wheat prices, which have pushed up bread prices by 30 percent in the past two weeks.

The U.S. Agriculture Department, which suspended export certificates for wheat sales to Turkey two weeks ago in response to the new policy, said on Thursday it had stopped issuing certificates for all grain and oilseed exports.
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said he would meet Turkey's ambassador on Friday to discuss the issue.
Traders and farm experts say it is almost impossible to guarantee complete absence of the fungus anywhere in the world.

"The wheat produced in Turkey also contains ergot, and in most places at levels not acceptable by the Turkish quarantine rule itself," said Ilker Tanik, secretary-general of the Turkish Millers' Association.
Millers and traders said Turkey's plans to import up to 500,000 tonnes of wheat to curb the rise in bread prices would also fall under the harsh scrutiny of the import restrictions.

"I wonder how the Turkish Grain Board will manage to get clearance for its massive imports at a time when smaller batches of wheat get detained for weeks at ports?" said a Western trader based in Turkey.
Turkish importers, whose U.S. milling wheat cargoes have been held at ports for disease checks for two weeks, said they were allowed to bring the wheat in following health clearances.

"We have been told by the authorities that we can transport the wheat into our mills," said Erhan Gencer of the milling company Marmara Un Sanayi, which had 18,000 tonnes waiting at the western Tekirdag port.

"Our wheat had 0.018 percent ergot fungus, which is below the new limit of 0.02 percent. But we were also told we can carry it to the mill only after making sure that no wheat spills out of trucks," he said.
Two other importers, who declined to be named, said they got clearance for cargoes of 15,000 tonnes and 18,000 tonnes at Derince and Iskenderun ports respectively.

Quarantine officials later said importers should sieve out contaminated grain at ports, but the importers objected, saying the ports did not have the technology. Market sources say about 100,000 tonnes are en route to Turkey from the United States.
